subject: Astronomy & Space
title: SN 1987A: The Supernova We Watched
description: Learn SN 1987A: The Supernova We Watched in one minute.

hook.text: On February 23, 1987, a star exploded in a nearby galaxy. It was the closest supernova in 400 years.

buildup.text: Astronomers detected neutrinos from the blast hours before the light arrived—confirming supernova theory.

discovery.text: The exploding star was Sanduleak −69° 202, a blue supergiant. Theorists had predicted only red supergiants could blow.

twist.text: The neutrino burst lasted 13 seconds but carried 99% of the explosion's energy. Light carried almost none.

climax.text: Decades later, dust is forming in the debris. A new generation of planets may someday emerge from the wreckage.

punchline.text: We watched a star die in real time. It rewrote the textbooks.

quiz.question: What surprised scientists about SN 1987A?
options: A blue supergiant exploded, not a red one as theory predicted
It produced no visible light at all
It occurred in our own Milky Way galaxy

details.summary: Supernova 1987A in the Large Magellanic Cloud was the nearest observed supernova since 1604 and the first visible to the naked eye in the modern telescope era. It confirmed theoretical models of core-collapse supernovae and marked the first detection of neutrinos from a stellar explosion.
details.whyItMatters: SN 1987A validated decades of supernova theory in real time. The neutrino detection confirmed that core collapse produces a neutrino burst, inaugurating neutrino astronomy as a tool for studying stellar interiors.
takeaways: SN 1987A was the nearest supernova since 1604
It was the first to produce detected neutrinos
It confirmed core-collapse supernova theoretical models

faq.question: How far away was SN 1987A?
faq.answer: About 168,000 light-years, in the Large Magellanic Cloud — a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Despite this enormous distance, it was visible to the naked eye for months. The neutrinos arrived hours before the light, having escaped the collapsing core before the shockwave reached the surface.

faq.question: Did SN 1987A leave a neutron star?
faq.answer: For decades, the remnant was hidden in dust. In 2019, observations suggested a compact object consistent with a neutron star exists at the center. Recent JWST observations have strengthened this evidence. Confirming it would complete our understanding of SN 1987A's aftermath.
